description: We are a team that loves innovative projects and experiments.
summary:
Moon Shift is an interactive browser-based lunar mission simulator. Players must keep a crew of three astronauts alive for seven simulated days on the Moon. Players take charge of a lunar base, juggling the needs of water, energy and crew safety. Decisions made to deal with daily emergencies have immediate, and sometimes lagged, consequences.

The project aims to address the challenge of developing a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer to transform complex space exploration concepts into a fun and accessible experience for young students aged 7–12. Real engineering trade-offs face the players: guarding astronauts against radiation might eat up power, and saving resources now may lead to problems later on in the mission.

Moon Shift also leverages NASA’s DONKI space weather data to correlate simulated mission events with real solar activity. The project combines interactive gameplay and scientific context to immerse learners in systems thinking, critical thinking, and problem-solving, and to expose the next generation to the challenges of living and working off Earth.
details:
Moon Shift

Mission Overview

Moon Shift is a browser game for children aged 7–12 where you command a small lunar outpost with three astronauts: Nova the engineer, Kai the doctor and Zuri the gardener. The goal is to keep the crew alive for seven simulated days by managing three resources: Water, Energy and Crew Safety. Each starts at 65 out of 100, and ordinary life on the outpost uses up a little of each every day. If any of them reaches zero, the mission ends. Survive the seventh day and the mission succeeds.

Daily Challenges & Decision-Making

Each day brings one challenge, picked from 16 scenarios we wrote: moon dust covering the solar panels, a solar storm, an oxygen system failure, a water shortage, a long lunar night, a struggling greenhouse, an overheating machine, a lost radio link, freezing temperatures, a micrometeoroid hole, a moonquake, a radiation shield upgrade, and a few quieter days such as a homesick crew or a lucky find of ice. The player gets three options, and every option helps one thing while costing another. To brush dust off the panels you can send an astronaut on a spacewalk, which gives power but risks the crew. You can also wash the panels, which uses water. Or you can leave the dust and lose energy. The buttons show only which resources a choice touches, not whether it goes up or down, so players have to reason about it. After choosing, they see what happened, how the numbers moved, and a short “Space science” explanation in plain English.

Consequences Beyond Today

Some consequences do not appear right away. If you finish a repair outside during a solar storm, the crew feels unwell the next day. If you open emergency oxygen tanks, two days later the water drops, because the game explains that oxygen can be made by splitting water. If you postpone checking the pipes after a moonquake, a hidden leak costs water overnight. These effects show up in an “Overnight” box, so players see cause and effect across days instead of only within one decision. The order of events is random without repeats. To keep it fair, day 1 is never an emergency, a calm day always appears by day 4, and when a resource is running low the game tends to offer an event that gives a way to refill it. At the end, the results screen shows the crew’s condition, the final levels, a label for the player’s style (crew-first, resource saver, risk taker or balanced) and one or two science lessons based on how they played.

NASA DONKI Integration

The game also connects to NASA’s DONKI space weather database. In the browser, it requests solar flare (FLR) and coronal mass ejection (CME) records from the CCMC DONKI API. The API limits each request to 30 days, so the game makes two requests per type to cover the last 60 days. It then shows the most recent event in a “NASA Reality Check” panel: the event type, date, location or speed when available, and a short kid-friendly explanation of why scientists watch it. We want to be clear about what this is. DONKI reports events on the Sun. It does not measure radiation on the Moon’s surface, and our game does not either. The panel is styled differently from the rest of the interface (a dashed amber border and a “Real data” label), and it states that the game’s numbers are made up. The real data does not change the game’s numbers or choose its events. Its job is context: two scenarios, the solar storm and the radiation shield, carry an “Inspired by real space weather” tag, so a child can connect a made-up emergency to something the Sun actually does. If NASA cannot be reached, the panel shows a friendly message and a retry button, and the game keeps working.

Educational Benefits & Impact

We hope Moon Shift helps young learners feel an idea that is hard to get from facts alone: space missions are about trade-offs. Water cools machines, makes oxygen and can shield people from radiation, so spending it in one place leaves less for another. Power has to be planned around a two-week lunar night. A fix that saves the crew today can cost something tomorrow. Children practice systems thinking, cause-and-effect reasoning, critical thinking and resource management by making these choices themselves. Failure is written to encourage another try rather than to punish: the end message says mission control brought the crew home safely and invites players to go again. The game runs in any modern browser with no installation, no account and no saved data, so it is easy to use in a classroom or at home.

Technology & Development

We built it with TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion and Lucide icons, and deployed it on Vercel. The game logic is kept separate from the interface: a pure engine, a separate events file, and a NASA module with its own timeout and error handling. We also use Vercel Analytics. The code is public on GitHub under a public-domain license.

Creative Design & Audio Experience

The creative part for us was making every day look and sound different. Each of the 16 events has its own animated scene, drawn in code with SVG and CSS rather than image files: a dusty solar array, a leaking life-support unit, a dried-up water tank, a drooping greenhouse, and more. The scene reacts to the player’s decision: the dust disappears, astronauts walk into the shelter, a leak stops. Each type of event also enters with its own transition. The sound is generated live with the Web Audio API. Five synthesized music moods (menu, gameplay, emergency, victory and failure) crossfade as the situation changes, and about 30 procedural sound effects (for example a leak, a power shutdown, a pipe, a heater) are timed to events and choices. Nothing plays until the player presses Start Mission, and players can control music and effects volume separately or mute them.

Accessibility, Scientific Accuracy & Design Considerations

When designing, we considered our audience first. The text is short, in plain English and explains words like “radiation” and “solar storm” in context. Buttons are large, and effects are shown with icons and text, not color alone. The game supports keyboard use and visible focus, screen reader labels for the bars and scenes, and the browser’s reduced-motion setting. We kept the science honest: the numbers are simplified for gameplay, the game is not a physically accurate mission simulator, and real NASA information is always separated from simulated values. We also had to work within limits: a small team, no backend, and a free public NASA API. We chose a static web app, because it is simple to deploy and share. During development we tuned the difficulty by running automated playthroughs, so that some strategies clearly work better but no single choice always wins.
